F1.quote: Let us now discuss sophistic refutations, i.e. what appear to be refutations but are really fallacies instead.
F1.claim: The treatise's subject is sophistic refutations, defined as apparent refutations that are really fallacies.
F1.lineage: subject: sophistic refutations are apparent refutations

F2.quote: reasoning rests on certain statements such that they involve necessarily the assertion of something other than what has been stated, through what has been stated: refutation is reasoning involving the contradictory of the given conclusion.
F2.claim: Reasoning is defined as statements necessarily entailing something other than what was stated, and refutation as reasoning involving the contradictory of the given conclusion.

F3.quote: That some reasonings are genuine, while others seem to be so but are not, is evident.
F3.claim: Some reasonings are genuine while others only seem so, through a likeness between genuine and sham.

F4.quote: of these the most prolific and usual domain is the argument that turns upon names only.
F4.claim: The most prolific domain of apparent refutation is argument turning on names alone.
F4.lineage: names as chief source of apparent refutation

F5.quote: For names are finite and so is the sum-total of formulae, while things are infinite in number. Inevitably, then, the same formulae, and a single name, have a number of meanings.
F5.claim: Because names are finite and things infinite, single names and formulae must have multiple meanings, which makes equivocal argument possible.
F5.lineage: finite names vs infinite things explains equivocation

F6.quote: the art of the sophist is the semblance of wisdom without the reality
F6.claim: The sophist's art is defined as the semblance of wisdom without the reality.

F7.quote: contentious arguments are those that reason or appear to reason to a conclusion from premisses that appear to be generally accepted but are not so.
F7.claim: Contentious arguments are defined as those that reason or appear to reason from premisses that seem generally accepted but are not.

F8.quote: The subject, then, of demonstrative arguments has been discussed in the Analytics, while that of dialectic arguments and examination-arguments has been discussed elsewhere
F8.claim: Demonstrative, dialectical and examination arguments are treated elsewhere, so this work turns to arguments used in competitions and contests.
F8.lineage: scope relative to Analytics and Topics

F9.quote: These are five in number, refutation, fallacy, paradox, solecism, and fifthly to reduce the opponent in the discussion to babbling
F9.claim: Contentious disputants have five aims: refutation, fallacy, paradox, solecism and reducing the opponent to babbling.

F10.quote: For they choose if possible plainly to refute the other party, or as the second best to show that he is committing some fallacy, or as a third best to lead him into paradox
F10.claim: The five aims are ranked, with refutation preferred first and repetition a last resort.

F11.quote: There are two styles of refutation: for some depend on the language used, while some are independent of language.
F11.claim: Refutations divide into those depending on language and those independent of it.

F12.quote: they are ambiguity, amphiboly, combination, division of words, accent, form of expression.
F12.claim: There are six language-dependent fallacies, a number assured by induction and by syllogistic proof.

F13.quote: Of fallacies, on the other hand, that are independent of language there are seven kinds:
F13.claim: There are seven kinds of fallacy independent of language: accident, qualified/absolute, ignorance of refutation, consequent, begging the question, false cause, many questions as one.

F14.quote: 'Those learn who know: for it is those who know their letters who learn the letters dictated to them'. For to 'learn' is ambiguous
F14.claim: The argument 'those learn who know' exemplifies ambiguity, since 'learn' means both to understand and to acquire knowledge.

F15.quote: Fallacies, then, that depend on Accident occur whenever any attribute is claimed to belong in like manner to a thing and to its accident.
F15.claim: Fallacies of accident occur when an attribute is claimed to belong alike to a thing and to its accident.

F16.quote: 'If Coriscus be different from "man", he is different from himself: for he is a man'
F16.claim: The Coriscus argument exemplifies the fallacy of accident.

F17.quote: deception comes about because we cannot distinguish the sameness and otherness of terms, i.e. their unity and multiplicity
F17.claim: Accident fallacies deceive because we cannot distinguish sameness and otherness of terms, i.e. unity and multiplicity.
F17.lineage: cause of deception in accident fallacies

F18.quote: the deception consists in the smallness of the difference involved
F18.claim: Qualified/absolute, begging-the-question, false-cause and many-questions fallacies deceive because the difference is small.
F18.lineage: smallness of difference as cause of deception

F19.quote: for the consequent is a branch of Accident.
F19.claim: The fallacy of the consequent is treated as a branch of the fallacy of accident.

F20.quote: By a sophistical refutation and syllogism I mean not only a syllogism or refutation which appears to be valid but is not, but also one which, though it is valid, only appears to be appropriate to the thing in question.
F20.claim: Sophistical refutation is defined to include both apparently valid invalid arguments and valid arguments that only appear appropriate to the subject.

F21.quote: Now the art of examining is a branch of dialectic: and this may prove a false conclusion because of the ignorance of the answerer.
F21.claim: The art of examination is a branch of dialectic and may reach a false conclusion through the answerer's ignorance.

F22.quote: Sophistic refutations on the other hand, even though they prove the contradictory of his thesis, do not make clear whether he is ignorant
F22.claim: Sophistic refutations, even when they prove the contradictory of the thesis, do not show whether the answerer is ignorant.
F22.lineage: sophistic refutation fails to expose ignorance

F23.locus: Section 1 (end), on didactic and dialectical argument
F23.quote: while he who argues didactically should not ask questions but make things clear himself, the other should merely ask questions.
F23.claim: Didactic argument explains rather than asks questions, while dialectical argument only asks them.

F24.quote: to claim a 'Yes' or 'No' answer is the business not of a man who is showing something, but of one who is holding an examination.
F24.claim: Demanding a yes/no answer belongs to the examiner, not to one who is demonstrating.

F25.quote: He, then, is a dialectician who regards the common principles with their application to the particular matter in hand, while he who only appears to do this is a sophist.
F25.claim: The dialectician is defined as one who applies common principles to the matter in hand, the sophist as one who only appears to.

F26.quote: But Bryson's method of squaring the circle, even if the circle is thereby squared, is still sophistical because it does not conform to the subject in hand.
F26.claim: Bryson's squaring of the circle is sophistical because it does not conform to the subject, even if it succeeds; false geometrical diagrams such as Hippocrates' are not contentious.
F26.lineage: Bryson's squaring of the circle is sophistical

F27.quote: any reasoning that merely appears to conform to the subject in hand, even though it be genuine reasoning, is a contentious argument
F27.claim: Any reasoning merely appearing to conform to the subject, even if genuine, is contentious.
F27.lineage: contentious argument includes valid but inappropriate reasoning

F28.quote: the contentious reasoner will not be given to misreasoning from any definite class of principles, but will deal with every class.
F28.claim: The contentious reasoner misreasons from every class of principles, unlike the drawer of a false diagram, who is confined to one subject.

F29.quote: it is possible from these general principles to hold an examination on everything, and that there should be a definite art of so doing, and, moreover, an art which is not of the same kind as those which demonstrate.
F29.claim: General principles allow examination on any subject and so permit a definite art of examination distinct from demonstrative arts.
F29.lineage: general principles ground the art of examination

F30.quote: that it belongs to the dialectician to study these, and to be able to effect them, is not difficult to see: for the investigation of premisses comprises the whole of this study.
F30.claim: The dialectician is the one to study and be able to produce sophistical refutations, since investigating premisses comprises the whole of the study.

F31.quote: people are more inclined to make mistakes when they talk at large, and they talk at large when they have no defini
F31.claim: Questioning without reference to a definite subject best induces fallacy and paradox, since people err more when they talk at large.

F32.quote: Aristotle’s logic, especially his theory of the syllogism, has had an unparalleled influence on the history of Western thought.
F32.claim: Aristotle's logic, especially the syllogism theory, has had unparalleled influence on Western thought.

F33.quote: This article is written from the latter perspective. As such, it is about Aristotle’s logic, which is not always the same thing as what has been called “Aristotelian” logic.
F33.claim: The article adopts the modern formal-techniques perspective and distinguishes Aristotle's logic from what has been called 'Aristotelian' logic.
F33.lineage: article scope: Aristotle's logic vs Aristotelian logic

F34.quote: More recent scholarship has often applied the very techniques of mathematical logic to Aristotle’s theories, revealing (in the opinion of many) a number of similarities of approach and interest between Aristotle and modern logicians.
F34.claim: Applying mathematical logic to Aristotle's theories has, in many scholars' opinion, revealed similarities with modern logicians.
F34.lineage: similarity of Aristotle and modern logic

F35.quote: Kant thought that Aristotle had discovered everything there was to know about logic
F35.claim: Kant held that Aristotle had discovered everything there was to know about logic.

F36.quote: The ancient commentators grouped together several of Aristotle’s treatises under the title Organon (“Instrument”) and regarded them as comprising his logical works:
F36.claim: Ancient commentators grouped certain treatises, including On Sophistical Refutations, as the Organon, his logical works.

F37.quote: Aristotle himself never uses this term, nor does he give much indication that these particular treatises form some kind of group
F37.claim: Aristotle never uses the term Organon and gives little sign that the treatises form a group.

F38.quote: On Sophistical Refutations is a final section, or an appendix, to the Topics
F38.claim: On Sophistical Refutations is a final section or appendix to the Topics.
F38.lineage: Sophistical Refutations as appendix to Topics

F39.quote: In these exchanges, one participant took the role of answerer, the other the role of questioner.
F39.claim: Academy dialectical exchanges, the practice the Topics (and so its appendix) presupposes, had questioner and answerer roles.

F40.quote: to refute ( elenchein ) the answerer’s position
F40.claim: The questioner's aim was to refute the answerer's thesis by deriving a contradiction from concessions.

F41.claim: The article has a dedicated section on sophistical arguments, listed after dialectic and rhetoric.

F42.locus: closing recapitulation of the original purpose
F42.quote: Προειλόμεθα μὲν οὖν εὑρεῖν δύναμίν τινα συλλογιστικὴν περὶ τοῦ προβληθέντος ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων ὡς ἐνδοξοτάτων
F42.claim: The treatise's stated aim was to find a capacity for reasoning (syllogistic) on any proposed problem from the most reputable available premises.

F43.locus: closing recapitulation of the original purpose
F43.quote: τοῦτο γὰρ ἔργον ἐστὶ τῆς διαλεκτικῆς καθ᾿ αὑτὴν καὶ τῆς πειραστικῆς
F43.claim: Finding such a capacity is the proper work of dialectic in itself and of examination (peirastic).

F44.locus: closing recapitulation of the original purpose
F44.quote: Ἐπεὶ δὲ προσκατασκευάζεται πρὸς αὐτὴν διὰ τὴν τῆς σοφιστικῆς γειτνίασιν, ὡς οὐ μόνον πεῖραν δύναται λαβεῖν διαλεκτικῶς ἀλλὰ καὶ ὡς εἰδώς
F44.claim: Because of sophistic's proximity, the discipline is fitted out so as to be able to test dialectically and also to proceed as one who knows.

F45.locus: closing recapitulation of the original purpose
F45.quote: ὅπως λόγον ὑπέχοντες φυλάξομεν τὴν θέσιν ὡς δι᾿ ἐνδοξοτάτων ὁμοτρόπως
F45.claim: A further aim is how, when giving an account, to guard one's thesis through the most reputable premises in the same manner.

F46.locus: closing recapitulation of the original purpose
F46.quote: ἐπεὶ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο Σωκράτης ἠρώτα, ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ ἀπεκρίνετο· ὡμολόγει γὰρ οὐκ εἰδέναι.
F46.claim: Socrates asked questions and did not answer because he admitted he did not know.
F46.lineage: Socrates asked and did not answer

F47.quote: Τὸν αὐτὸν γὰρ λόγον δεῖ καλεῖν τὸν παρὰ ταὐτὸ γινόμενον
F47.claim: An argument arising from the same source of fallacy must be called the same argument.
F47.lineage: identity of arguments by source of fallacy

F48.quote: ὁ αὐτὸς δὲ λόγος τοῖς μὲν παρὰ τὴν λέξιν τοῖς δὲ παρὰ τὸ συμβεβηκὸς τοῖς δὲ παρ᾿ ἕτερον δόξειεν ἂν εἶναι διὰ τὸ μεταφερόμενον ἕκαστον μὴ ὁμοίως εἶναι δῆλον.
F48.claim: The same argument may seem to different people to fall under language, accident or another source, because it is not equally clear when transferred.
F48.lineage: one argument classified differently by different people

F49.quote: Δεῖ δὲ καὶ κατανοεῖν ὅτι πάντων τῶν λόγων οἱ μέν εἰσι ῥᾴους κατιδεῖν οἱ δὲ χαλεπώτεροι, παρὰ τί καὶ ἐν τίνι παραλογίζονται τὸν ἀκούοντα
F49.claim: Some arguments are easier, others harder, to see through, as to what they deceive the hearer by and in.
F49.lineage: arguments differ in difficulty of detection

F50.quote: ὥσπερ δοκεῖ τρόπος εὐηθέστατος εἶναι τῶν παραλογισμῶν
F50.claim: Fallacies from homonymy are held to be the silliest mode of fallacy.

F51.quote: καὶ γὰρ οἱ λόγοι σχεδὸν οἱ γελοῖοι πάντες εἰσὶ παρὰ τὴν λέξιν
F51.claim: Almost all jocular arguments depend on language.

F52.quote: Τὰ δὲ καὶ τοὺς ἐμπειροτάτους φαίνεται λανθάνειν· σημεῖον δὲ τούτων ὅτι μάχονται πολλάκις περὶ τῶν ὀνομάτων
F52.claim: Some homonymy-based fallacies escape even the most experienced, as shown by their frequent disputes about names.

F53.quote: οἱ δὲ τὸν Ζήνωνος λόγον καὶ Παρμενίδου λύουσι διὰ τὸ πολλαχῶς φάναι τὸ ἓν λέγεσθαι καὶ τὸ ὄν.
F53.claim: Some solve the argument of Zeno and Parmenides by saying that 'one' and 'being' are said in many ways.
F53.lineage: Zeno/Parmenides solved by multiple senses of one and being

F54.quote: καὶ λαβεῖν ἐν τίνι γένει, καὶ πότερον ἔλεγχος ἢ οὐκ ἔλεγχος, οὐ ῥᾴδιον ὁμοίως περὶ πάντων.
F54.claim: Determining the kind of fallacy and whether an argument is a refutation or not is not equally easy in all cases.

F55.quote: Ἔστι δὲ δριμὺς λόγος ὅστις ἀπορεῖν ποιεῖ μάλιστα· δάκνει γὰρ οὗτος μάλιστα.
F55.claim: A pungent argument is one that most produces perplexity; it bites most.

F56.quote: Ἀπορία δ᾿ ἐστὶ διττή, ἡ μὲν ἐν τοῖς συλλελογισμένοις, ὅ τι ἀνέλῃ τις τῶν ἐρωτημάτων, ἡ δ᾿ ἐν τοῖς ἐριστικοῖς, πῶς εἴπῃ τις τὸ προταθέν.
F56.claim: Perplexity is twofold: in valid arguments, which question to remove; in eristic ones, how to state the proposition.

F57.quote: Ἔστι δὲ συλλογιστικὸς μὲν λόγος δριμύτατος, ἂν ἐξ ὅτι μάλιστα δοκούντων ὅτι μάλιστα ἔνδοξον ἀναιρῇ.
F57.claim: The most pungent valid argument is one that overturns a maximally reputable view from maximally reputable premises.

F58.quote: Τῶν δ᾿ ἐριστικῶν δριμύτατος μὲν ὁ πρῶτον εὐθὺς ἄδηλος πότερον συλλελόγισται ἢ οὔ
F58.claim: The most pungent eristic argument is one where it is at first unclear whether it is a valid deduction and whether the solution lies in falsity or division.

F59.claim: An argument that is not a valid deduction is sometimes not to be despised.

F60.quote: ἀλλ᾿ ὁ μὲν λόγος ἐπιεικής, ὁ δ᾿ ἐρωτῶν ἠρώτηκεν οὐ καλῶς.
F60.claim: Where the missing element is external, the argument is decent but the questioner has questioned badly.

F61.quote: ὥσπερ λύειν ὁτὲ μὲν πρὸς τὸν λόγον ὁτὲ δὲ πρὸς τὸν ἐρωτῶντα καὶ τὴν ἐρώτησιν ὁτὲ δὲ πρὸς οὐδέτερον τούτων
F61.claim: A solution may be directed at the argument, at the questioner and question, or at neither; likewise questioning may be directed at the thesis, the answerer or the time.
F61.lineage: solutions directed at argument, questioner or neither

F62.quote: Ἐκ πόσων μὲν οὖν καὶ ποίων γίνονται τοῖς διαλεγομένοις οἱ παραλογισμοί, καὶ πῶς δείξομέν τε ψευδόμενον
F62.claim: The author summarises what has been covered: sources of fallacies, refuting and leading to paradox, premises, ordering of questions, uses, answering, and solving arguments.

F63.quote: Ὅτι μὲν οὖν ἔχει τέλος ἱκανῶς ἃ προειλόμεθα, φανερόν
F63.claim: It is clear that what was undertaken has been adequately completed.

F64.quote: Ταύτης δὲ τῆς πραγματείας οὐ τὸ μὲν ἦν τὸ δ᾿ οὐκ ἦν προεξειργασμένον, ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν.
F64.claim: For this inquiry nothing at all had been worked out previously.
F64.lineage: no predecessors for the theory of syllogism and refutation

F65.quote: περὶ δὲ τοῦ συλλογίζεσθαι παντελῶς οὐδὲν εἴχομεν πρότερον ἄλλο λέγειν, ἀλλ᾿ ἢ τριβῇ ζητοῦντες πολὺν χρόνον ἐπονοῦμεν.
F65.claim: On reasoning there was nothing previously to cite; the author laboured long by trial and inquiry.
F65.lineage: no predecessors for the theory of syllogism and refutation

F66.quote: Μέγιστον γὰρ ἴσως ἀρχὴ παντός, ὥσπερ λέγεται· διὸ καὶ χαλεπώτατον
F66.claim: A beginning is perhaps the greatest part of everything, and hence the hardest; discoveries made from scratch grow little at first but are far more useful than later growth.

F67.quote: Τισίας μὲν μετὰ τοὺς πρώτους, Θρασύμαχος δὲ μετὰ Τισίαν, Θεόδωρος δὲ μετὰ τοῦτον
F67.claim: Rhetoric grew by succession: Tisias after the first, Thrasymachus after Tisias, Theodorus after him.

F68.locus: closing, on paid teachers of eristic
F68.quote: Καὶ γὰρ τῶν περὶ τοὺς ἐριστικοὺς λόγους μισθαρνούντων ὁμοία τις ἦν ἡ παίδευσις τῇ Γοργίου πραγματείᾳ.
F68.claim: The paid teachers of eristic arguments used an education similar to Gorgias' practice, handing over arguments to memorise.
F68.lineage: paid teachers taught by memorised arguments

F69.locus: closing, on paid teachers of eristic
F69.quote: οὐ γὰρ τέχνην ἀλλὰ τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς τέχνης διδόντες παιδεύειν ὑπελάμβανον
F69.claim: Their teaching was quick but artless: they gave the products of an art, not the art, and thought they were educating.
F69.lineage: teaching products of the art rather than the art

F70.quote: ὥσπερ ἂν εἴ τις ἐπιστήμην φάσκων παραδώσειν ἐπὶ τὸ μηδὲν πονεῖν τοὺς πόδας, εἶτα σκυτοτομικὴν μὲν μὴ διδάσκοι
F70.claim: Like someone promising to spare the feet pain who gives many kinds of shoes but does not teach shoemaking: he met the need but passed on no art.

F71.quote: δεῖ δ᾿ ἡμᾶς μὴ λεληθέναι τὸ συμβεβηκὸς περὶ ταύτην τὴν πραγματείαν.
F71.claim: We must keep in mind the condition attending this inquiry, namely that it began from nothing.
F71.lineage: limit: pioneering status of the work

F72.quote: λοιπὸν ἂν εἴη πάντων ὑμῶν ἢ τῶν ἠκροαμένων ἔργον τοῖς μὲν παραλελειμμένοις τῆς μεθόδου συγγνώμην τοῖς δ᾿ εὑρημένοις πολλὴν ἔχειν χάριν.
F72.claim: If the method seems adequate given its starting point, it remains for the audience to forgive its omissions and be warmly grateful for what has been discovered.
F72.lineage: limit: pioneering status of the work
